title: Jackson v. Southfield Neighborhood Revitalization Initiative
description: Whether a governmental unit commits a taking under the Michigan Constitution when it acquires tax-foreclosed properties for the minimum bid through a right-of-first-refusal process, without a public auction, and whether subsequent statutory amendments regarding surplus proceeds apply retroactively.
plaintiff_argument: The governmental units' actions violated the Takings Clauses of the Michigan and United States Constitutions by acquiring properties for only the minimum bid without public auction, thus failing to provide just compensation for the surplus value, and that new statutes should apply retroactively.
defendant_argument: The governmental units initially argued lack of jurisdiction, standing, and res judicata, and later that Rafaeli did not apply retroactively and plaintiffs had no protected property interests; they also argued that amended MCL 211.78m should not apply retroactively. Oakland County conceded liability for the taking.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed in part and reversed in part, holding that a taking requiring just compensation occurred when the government obtained surplus value from foreclosed properties transferred for the minimum bid without public auction, that MCL 211.78t applies retroactively but is inapplicable to this case, and that amended MCL 211.78m applies prospectively only, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: Michigan Immigrant Rights Center v. Governor
description: Whether the Court of Claims Act's one-year notice provision applies to claims seeking prospective relief against state officers for alleged state and federal constitutional violations.
plaintiff_argument: The notice provision of the Court of Claims Act does not apply to claims for prospective relief against state officers, especially for constitutional claims, as it only applies to claims based on past harms, not future harms.
defendant_argument: The notice provision of the Court of Claims Act does apply to the plaintiff's suit, and the plaintiff failed to comply with it by not filing notice within one year of the claim accruing.
decision_outcome: The Michigan Supreme Court denied the plaintiff's application for leave to appeal, thereby upholding the Court of Appeals' decision that the notice provision of the Court of Claims Act applies to the plaintiff's suit for prospective relief, leading to the dismissal of the case.

title: People v. Armstrong
description: Whether the Michigan Regulation and Taxation of Marihuana Act (MRTMA) superseded the rule that the smell of marijuana alone establishes probable cause to search a motor vehicle.
plaintiff_argument: The smell of marijuana alone provided probable cause for a warrantless vehicle search under the Kazmierczak rule, or the gun was found in plain view during a lawful investigatory stop.
defendant_argument: The gun was discovered during an unconstitutional search, as the smell of marijuana alone no longer provides probable cause after the MRTMA.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision to suppress the evidence and dismiss the charges, ruling that the smell of marijuana alone no longer provides probable cause for a warrantless vehicle search.

title: People v. Taylor; People v. Czarnecki
description: Whether mandatorily subjecting 19- and 20-year-old defendants convicted of first-degree murder to a sentence of life without parole (LWOP) violates Michigan's constitutional prohibition against cruel or unusual punishment.
plaintiff_argument: The mandatory LWOP sentence for 19- and 20-year-olds is constitutional, as the Legislature's judgment on severe crimes should be respected, and Michigan's sentencing scheme is not an outlier compared to other jurisdictions.
defendant_argument: The mandatory LWOP sentence for 19- and 20-year-olds is unconstitutional because it is disproportionate, fails to consider youth-related mitigating factors due to late-adolescent brain development, and prevents rehabilitation, violating Michigan's cruel or unusual punishment clause.
decision_outcome: The Michigan Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, vacated the defendants' mandatory LWOP sentences for first-degree murder, and remanded the cases for individualized resentencing, extending the protections previously granted to 18-year-olds to 19- and 20-year-old offenders.

title: Heos v. City of East Lansing
description: Whether the franchise fee imposed by the City of East Lansing on electric utility consumers, collected by the Lansing Board of Water and Light (LBWL), constitutes an unlawful tax requiring voter approval under the Headlee Amendment, or a legitimate user fee.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the franchise fee is an illegal tax violating the Headlee Amendment and other state laws because it was not approved by voters, and that he is a taxpayer with a timely claim.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the franchise fee is a legitimate user fee, or alternatively, that the plaintiff is not a "taxpayer" but a "member of the public," making his Headlee Amendment claims time-barred.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment, ruling that the franchise fee is an unauthorized tax violating the Headlee Amendment and that the plaintiff is a taxpayer with a viable claim, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: People v. Poole
description: Whether People v Parks, which held that mandatory life-without-parole sentences for 18-year-old homicide offenders violated the Michigan Constitution, applies retroactively to cases where the period for direct review had expired when Parks was decided. The prosecution argued it should not apply retroactively, while the defendant argued it should.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that the Court of Appeals erred by concluding that Parks applied retroactively.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that Parks applied retroactively, entitling him to resentencing.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court held that the Parks ruling, which found mandatory life-without-parole sentences for 18-year-old homicide offenders unconstitutional, applies retroactively, affirming the Court of Appeals' decision to vacate the defendant's sentence and remand for resentencing.

title: People v. Loew
description: Whether ex parte communications between a trial judge and the prosecutor warrant granting the defendant a new trial under MCR 6.431(B), with the plaintiff arguing such communications were harmless and the defendant arguing they violated his due process rights and created an appearance of impropriety.
plaintiff_argument: The ex parte communications were for administrative purposes, did not show actual bias, did not affect the jury, and did not violate the defendant's constitutional rights, therefore a new trial is not warranted.
defendant_argument: The trial judge's ex parte communications with the prosecutor violated judicial conduct, created an appearance of impropriety, and deprived him of his constitutional rights to a fair trial, to be present, and to counsel, thus warranting a new trial.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, which had reversed the trial court's grant of a new trial, thereby denying the defendant a new trial.

title: O’Halloran v. Sec. of State
description: Whether the Secretary of State's 2022 election manual provisions regarding challenger credentials, challenger liaisons, and challenge categorization are consistent with Michigan Election Law and if they require formal rulemaking under the APA.
plaintiff_argument: The manual's provisions conflict with Michigan Election Law and/or constitute administrative rules that were not properly promulgated under the APA.
defendant_argument: The manual's provisions are consistent with Michigan Election Law and fall under exceptions to APA rulemaking requirements as interpretive statements or forms with instructions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed in part, reversed in part, and vacated in part, finding some manual provisions lawful, some unlawful, and one moot due to statutory amendments.

title: People v. Neilly
description: Whether the trial court violated federal and state constitutional prohibitions on ex post facto laws by ordering the defendant to pay restitution under current statutes during resentencing, rather than the statutes in effect at the time of his crimes.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the trial court's application of the current restitution statutes was proper because restitution is a civil remedy and not a criminal punishment, thus not violating ex post facto prohibitions.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court's order to pay restitution under current statutes violated ex post facto clauses because it constituted an increased criminal punishment compared to the statutes in effect at the time of his crime.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the trial court's restitution order, holding that restitution under the current statutes is a civil remedy, not a criminal punishment, and therefore its application did not violate ex post facto prohibitions.

title: People v. Lymon
description: Whether requiring a defendant to register as a sex offender under the Sex Offenders Registration Act (SORA) for a non-sexual crime, such as unlawful imprisonment of a minor, constitutes cruel or unusual punishment under the Michigan Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that SORA registration for non-sexual crimes is a reasonable measure for public protection and does not constitute cruel or unusual punishment, and cross-appealed the removal of the defendant from SORA.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that his inclusion on the sex-offender registry under SORA for a non-sexual crime constitutes cruel or unusual punishment in violation of the Michigan Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the imposition of the 2021 SORA on non-sexual offenders constitutes cruel or unusual punishment under the Michigan Constitution and affirmed the judgment to remove the defendant and other similarly situated offenders from the sex-offender registry.

title: Mothering Justice v. Attorney General
description: Whether the Michigan Legislature can adopt an initiative petition and then amend it in the same legislative session, given the constitutional provisions for direct democracy.
plaintiff_argument: The Legislature's 'adopt-and-amend' practice is unconstitutional under Article 2, § 9 of the Michigan Constitution, which outlines only three options for handling initiative petitions, none of which permit adopting and then amending in the same session.
defendant_argument: The Michigan Constitution does not expressly prohibit the Legislature from adopting and amending an initiative proposal in the same legislative session, and therefore, the Legislature is free to do so under its general legislative power.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment, declared 2018 PA 368 and 2018 PA 369 unconstitutional, and ordered 2018 PA 337 and 2018 PA 338 to go into effect 205 days after July 31, 2024, with a revised schedule for minimum wage increases and inflation adjustments.

title: Planned Parenthood of Michigan v. Attorney General of the State of Michigan
description: Whether MCL 750.14, which prohibits all abortions except those performed to preserve the life of a woman, is constitutional under the Michigan Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that MCL 750.14 violates the Due Process Clause by infringing on the fundamental rights to bodily integrity and privacy, and the Equal Protection Clause by creating an illegal sex-based classification, under the Michigan Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that MCL 750.14 is constitutional, asserting that Michigan's Due Process and Equal Protection clauses are coextensive with federal interpretations (post-Dobbs) and do not include a right to abortion, and that the law is not a sex-based classification.
decision_outcome: The court declared MCL 750.14 unconstitutional on its face and permanently enjoined its enforcement.

title: People v. Posey
description: Whether a witness's first-time in-court identification of a defendant, after prior failed pretrial identifications, violates due process, and whether appellate courts can review sentences that fall within statutory guidelines for reasonableness.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the in-court identification was permissible due to no improper police activity and that MCL 769.34(10) requires appellate courts to affirm within-guidelines sentences, precluding substantive review.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that his due-process rights were violated by the unreliable first-time in-court identification and that MCL 769.34(10) impermissibly restricts appellate review of within-guidelines sentences, which should be reviewed for proportionality.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the defendant's convictions, finding no plain error or ineffective assistance of counsel regarding the in-court identification, but reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment on sentencing, holding that within-guidelines sentences are subject to appellate review for reasonableness and remanding the case for that review.

title: Mt. Clemens Recreational Bowl v. Director of the Department of Health & Human Services
description: Whether the state's COVID-19 shutdown orders constituted an unconstitutional taking of private property or actionable torts, and whether the case should have been transferred for a jury trial.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the state's COVID-19 shutdown orders constituted an unconstitutional regulatory taking of their business property without just compensation and actionable torts, and that they had a right to a jury trial in circuit court.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Court of Claims had exclusive jurisdiction, the shutdown orders were a valid exercise of police power for public health and not a compensable taking, and officials were immune from tort liability.
decision_outcome: The Court of Appeals affirmed the Court of Claims' order denying the plaintiffs' motion to transfer the case and granting summary disposition to the defendants.

title: The Gym 24/7 Fitness LLC v. State of Michigan
description: Whether a business owner is entitled to just compensation under the state or federal Takings Clause when the government properly exercises its police power to protect public health during a pandemic by temporarily closing the owner's business operations, with the plaintiff arguing for compensation and the defendant arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: The Gym argued that the Governor's temporary closure of fitness centers for a public purpose constituted a taking of their property interests, requiring just compensation under the US and Michigan Constitutions, regardless of the prudence or authority of the executive orders.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the exercise of police powers to protect public health and safety during a pandemic does not give rise to inverse condemnation or takings claims, and therefore, no compensation is owed for reasonable, temporary public health and safety measures.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Claims' decision and remanded for entry of judgment in favor of the State, ruling that the temporary closure of businesses for public health during a pandemic does not constitute a compensable taking.

title: People v. Johnson
description: Whether MCL 769.1k(1)(b)(iii), which allows trial courts to assess costs against convicted defendants to fund court operations, violates separation of powers principles and due process by creating a potential for judicial bias.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff implicitly argues that MCL 769.1k(1)(b)(iii) is constitutional and does not violate separation of powers or due process.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that MCL 769.1k(1)(b)(iii) is facially unconstitutional because it violates separation of powers and due process by creating a conflict of interest for judges.
decision_outcome: The Court vacated its prior order granting leave to appeal and denied the application for leave to appeal, effectively declining to review the constitutionality of the statute and allowing the lower court's decision (upholding the statute) to stand.

title: People v. Edwards
description: Whether MCL 769.1k(1)(b)(iii), which allows courts to impose costs on convicted defendants to fund court operations, violates separation-of-powers and due process principles by creating a potential for judicial bias.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argues that the statute is constitutional and does not create an unconstitutional potential for bias, as no actual bias has been demonstrated, and the funding mechanism is permissible.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the statute is unconstitutional because it creates a conflict of interest and a "potential for bias" for judges, infringing on due process and separation of powers by incentivizing convictions to fund courts.
decision_outcome: The Court vacated its prior order granting leave to appeal and denied the application for leave to appeal, stating they are no longer persuaded that the questions presented should be reviewed by this Court.

title: Reproductive Freedom for All v. Board of State Canvassers
description: Whether a constitutional amendment proposed by the Legislature under Const. 1963, art. 12, § 1, must be limited to a single purpose.
plaintiff_argument: The proposed amendment must be limited to a single purpose and fails this test because it addresses both term limits and financial disclosures.
defendant_argument: The text of Const. 1963, art. 12, § 1 does not establish a single-purpose test for amendments proposed by the Legislature.
decision_outcome: The Court denied the plaintiffs' complaint for mandamus and declaratory relief.

title: Promote The Vote 2022 v. Board of State Canvassers
description: Whether the Board of State Canvassers has a clear legal duty to certify the Promote the Vote petition for the ballot, given challenges that it fails to republish abrogated constitutional provisions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the proposed amendments would not abrogate any existing constitutional provisions and that the petition met all formal and signature requirements, thus the Board had a clear legal duty to certify it.
defendant_argument: The defendant (Defend Your Vote) argued that the petition failed to include all constitutional provisions that would be abrogated by the proposed amendments, as required by law, and therefore the Board had a clear legal duty to withhold certification.
decision_outcome: The court granted the complaint for mandamus and declaratory relief, ordering the Board of State Canvassers to certify the Promote the Vote petition for placement on the November 8 general election ballot.

title: Anderson v. Board of State Canvassers
description: Whether a constitutional amendment proposed by the Legislature under Const. 1963, art. 12, § 1 must be limited to a single purpose.
plaintiff_argument: The constitutional amendment proposed by the Legislature must be limited to a single purpose, and the current amendment (term limits and financial disclosures) fails this test as it has two purposes.
defendant_argument: The text of Const. 1963, art. 12, § 1 does not establish a single-purpose test for legislative-proposed amendments.
decision_outcome: The Court denied the requested relief, finding it was not persuaded to grant it.

title: People v. Boykin
description: Whether trial courts must consider a juvenile offender's youth as a mitigating factor when sentencing them to a term of years, and whether this consideration must be articulated on the record.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that trial courts are not required to consider a juvenile offender's youth as a mitigating factor or articulate it on the record when imposing a term-of-years sentence, as Miller v Alabama only applies to life-without-parole sentences.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that trial courts must consider a juvenile offender's youth as a mitigating factor when imposing a term-of-years sentence, and that failure to do so or articulate it on the record violates constitutional principles.
decision_outcome: The court held that trial courts must consider a juvenile offender's youth as a mitigating factor when sentencing them to term-of-years sentences, but this consideration need not be articulated on the record. The Court vacated the Court of Appeals judgments regarding sentencing challenges and remanded both cases for further consideration.

title: People v. Parks
description: Whether mandatory life imprisonment without the possibility of parole for 18-year-old homicide offenders violates the Eighth Amendment of the United States Constitution or the Michigan Constitution's prohibition against cruel or unusual punishment.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that mandatory life without parole for 18-year-old offenders is constitutional and that Miller's protections should not be extended to this age group.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that mandatory life without parole for 18-year-old offenders constitutes cruel and/or unusual punishment under both the federal and state Constitutions, seeking to extend Miller's protections.
decision_outcome: The court held that mandatorily subjecting 18-year-old defendants convicted of first-degree murder to a sentence of life imprisonment without the possibility of parole violates the principle of proportionality derived from the Michigan Constitution, constituting unconstitutionally cruel punishment, and remanded the case for resentencing.

title: People v. Stovall
description: Whether a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole for a defendant who committed second-degree murder while a juvenile constitutes cruel or unusual punishment and therefore violates Const 1963, art 1, § 16.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that the defendant's successive motion for relief from judgment was procedurally barred, his plea was not illusory, and his parolable life sentences were constitutional under both the Eighth Amendment and the Michigan Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that his plea was illusory, his sentences violated the Eighth Amendment and the Michigan Constitution's prohibition against cruel or unusual punishment, and effectively denied him a meaningful opportunity for release.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the defendant's sentence for second-degree murder and remanded the case for further proceedings, ruling that a parolable life sentence for a juvenile convicted of second-degree murder violates the Michigan Constitution.

title: Bauserman v. Unemployment Insurance Agency
description: Whether plaintiffs have a cognizable state constitutional-tort claim allowing them to recover a judicially inferred damages remedy for alleged due process violations by the Unemployment Insurance Agency.
plaintiff_argument: The Unemployment Insurance Agency violated their due-process rights by using an automated system (MiDAS) to determine benefit ineligibility, garnish wages, and seize tax refunds without adequate notice or opportunity to be heard, and no other adequate remedy existed.
defendant_argument: Plaintiffs' claims were not timely, they had alternative remedies under the Michigan Employment Security Act, and recognizing a cause of action for monetary damages for constitutional violations is beyond the court's authority and falls to the Legislature.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's denial of summary disposition for the defendant, holding that plaintiffs alleged a cognizable constitutional-tort claim for which they may recover monetary damages, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Detroit Caucus v. Independent Citizens Redistricting Commission
description: Whether the adopted redistricting plans violate federal laws, specifically the Voting Rights Act of 1965, by unlawfully diluting the voting power of minority groups.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs contend that the absence of an equivalent number of majority-minority districts in the adopted plans, compared to existing districts, constitutes unlawful vote dilution in violation of the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
defendant_argument: The defendant implicitly argues that the adopted plans comply with federal law and the VRA, as there was no strong basis in evidence to believe the Gingles preconditions for requiring race-based districts were met, and that white crossover voting ensures equal opportunity.
decision_outcome: The Court denied the relief requested and dismissed the first amended verified complaint, ruling that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that the Commission's adopted plans are noncompliant with federal law.

title: League of Women Voters of Michigan v. Secretary of State
description: Whether the 15% geographic cap on petition signatures and the precirculation affidavit requirement for paid circulators violate the Michigan Constitution and free speech rights, and whether the checkbox requirement for circulator status is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the 15% geographic-distribution requirement and the precirculation affidavit requirement for paid circulators were unconstitutional burdens on direct democracy and free speech, and that the checkbox requirement was also unconstitutional.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the challenged provisions of 2018 PA 608 were constitutional, falling within the Legislature's authority to regulate direct democracy and serving legitimate state interests in transparency and electoral integrity.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the 15% geographic cap on signatures and the precirculation affidavit requirement for paid circulators were unconstitutional, but the checkbox requirement passed constitutional muster, with the decision applied prospectively only.

title: The Detroit News,  Inc. v. Independent Citizens Redistricting Commission
description: Whether the Independent Citizens Redistricting Commission's attorney-client communications and work product, including a closed-session meeting recording and ten memoranda, are subject to public disclosure under constitutional transparency requirements, with plaintiffs arguing for disclosure and the Commission arguing for privilege.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs, a group of news organizations, sought the production of a recording from the Commission's closed-session meeting and disclosure of ten memoranda, contending that these materials constitute 'business' and 'supporting materials' that must be public under constitutional transparency mandates.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the Independent Citizens Redistricting Commission, asserted that the meeting and memoranda were privileged attorney-client communications, arguing that 'supporting materials' should be limited to factual information, not legal opinions, and that the meeting was related to inevitable litigation.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Commission's October 27 closed-session meeting violated the constitutional requirement to conduct all business at open meetings, and ordered the disclosure of the meeting recording. The court also ordered the publication of seven of the ten memoranda as 'supporting materials' used to develop redistricting plans, but found the remaining three were not 'supporting materials' and need not be disclosed.

title: Sheffield v. Detroit City Clerk
description: Whether the Detroit Charter Revision Commission may submit a proposed revised charter to voters without the Governor's approval, with the plaintiffs arguing that gubernatorial approval is required and the defendant arguing it is not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that MCL 117.22 requires the Governor's approval as a prerequisite for a proposed revised charter to be submitted to the electors, interpreting the statute's silence as vesting the Governor with an unfettered veto.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the Detroit Charter Revision Commission (DCRC), contended that the statute's silence on what happens when the Governor withholds approval for a charter revision means the revised charter can still be submitted to the electors without gubernatorial approval.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and the Wayne Circuit Court, ruling that the proposed revised charter could be submitted to voters without the Governor's approval.

title: People v. Washington
description: Whether the trial court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction when it resentenced the defendant in 2006 while the defendant's application for leave to appeal was still pending in the Supreme Court, with the plaintiff arguing it was merely an error in the exercise of jurisdiction and the defendant arguing it was a void action due to lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that the defendant's successive motion for relief from judgment was procedurally barred and that the trial court's error in 2006 was an error in the exercise of jurisdiction, not a lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, meaning the judgment was not void.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction when it resentenced him in 2006 because his application for leave to appeal was pending, rendering the 2006 judgment of sentence void, and such a jurisdictional defect could be raised in a successive motion.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment, holding that the trial court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction when it resentenced the defendant in 2006, making the 2006 judgment of sentence void, and affirmed the trial court's 2016 decision to vacate the void sentence and order resentencing.

title: Taxpayers for Michigan Constitutional Government v. State
description: Whether 'Proposal A' payments, state spending for state-mandated local services and activities under Const. 1963, art. 9, § 29, and state aid to Public School Academies (PSAs) should be included in the calculation of 'total state spending paid to all units of Local Government' under § 30 of the Headlee Amendment.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that 'Proposal A' payments, state spending for state-mandated local services, and state aid to Public School Academies (PSAs) should not be counted towards the 'total state spending paid to all units of Local Government' under § 30 of the Headlee Amendment, asserting that their inclusion violates the amendment's intent and proper classification.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that 'Proposal A' payments, state spending for state-mandated local services, and state aid to Public School Academies (PSAs) are properly counted as part of 'total state spending paid to all units of Local Government' under § 30 of the Headlee Amendment, as they fall within the constitutional definitions.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Proposal A payments and state spending for state-mandated local services are properly counted towards local government funding under the Headlee Amendment. It also ruled that Public School Academies (PSAs) are not 'school districts' or 'political subdivisions' for Headlee Amendment purposes, but remanded the issue of PSA funding to the Court of Appeals for further consideration if authorized by other local government units. The court also vacated and remanded the grant of mandamus relief.

title: People v. Pagano
description: Whether an anonymous 911 tip, without further corroboration of criminal activity by police, provides sufficient reasonable and articulable suspicion to justify a Fourth Amendment investigatory traffic stop.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the anonymous tip, which included identifying details of the vehicle, provided sufficient reasonable and articulable suspicion to justify the investigatory stop.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the anonymous tip, without independent police observation of criminal activity, did not provide reasonable and articulable suspicion for the traffic stop, thus violating the Fourth Amendment.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, holding that the investigatory stop did not comply with the Fourth Amendment because the police officer lacked reasonable and articulable suspicion of criminal activity.
